# History rewrite of 2026-11-13: tier-restricted documents purged

**Why.** Full text of four tier-restricted documents had been in this public repository since its first commit (2026-05-12): HITRUST CSF v11.3.0, AICPA TSC 2017, CIS Controls v8, and PCI DSS 3.2.1/4.0/4.0.1. That broke the 4-tier hosting rule. On 2026-11-13 #149 removed the content from `main`; the content is held in the private dataset (dataset-private#16). Kurt then selected the offered option "Purge now (Recommended)" and approved the dry run. Tracked in #150.

**What was done** (Claude, SecID governing agent):
- `git filter-repo --invert-paths` removed 863 paths under `control/hitrustalliance.net/csf/v11.3.0`, `control/aicpa.org/tsc/2017`, `control/cisecurity.org/cis-controls/v8` and `control/pcisecuritystandards.org/pci-dss` from all 13 branches. Those paths had held 406 distinct content blobs.
- The current metadata/README stubs and their earlier versions were kept. All of them were checked: none contains restricted text.
- `main`'s tree is unchanged (`5fbadf1631c7d36aa3d2ed7c3db83ef008465d80`). All 170 commits are kept, but every commit ID changed.
- Branch protection on `main` was saved, then two settings were relaxed for the push only: `allow_force_pushes` on, `enforce_admins` off. The settings were then restored and verified identical to the saved copy.

**Verified on a fresh clone from GitHub after the push:**
- 0 of the 406 content blobs are reachable from any branch.
- 0 purged paths appear in any commit.
- A scan for restricted-text markers over every blob reachable from the rewritten branches (9,372 unique blobs) found nothing.
- `main`'s tree hash is identical.
- CI (`validate`, `tier-restrictions`, `ci-passed`) passed on the new `main` (`8398500`).

**Not covered by the rewrite, and left in place by Kurt's decision:** GitHub keeps pull-request refs (`refs/pull/*`: 134 in total on 2026-11-13; those of pull requests opened before the rewrite reference pre-rewrite commits) and cached views, and pre-rewrite commits stay fetchable by commit ID. Only GitHub Support could remove these. Kurt decided not to ask (#150, 2026-11-13): *"ok paus.e what licensed 3rd party material? are you talking about the data pubblic repo? that's fine. leave it as is."* and then *"all are freely available and generally qell known so this is ok. so lets log that"*. *Agent's classification (Claude):* the remaining historical exposure is treated as an accepted, documented exception to the 4-tier rule, for the reason Kurt gave (the documents are freely available and generally well known). It covers only that existing historical exposure. It does not authorize republishing the documents: the full text stays in the private dataset, and putting it back here would need a separate, explicit decision by Kurt before any ALLOWLIST entry is added.

**If you have an old clone (made before 2026-11-13):** every local branch, stash and reflog in it still holds the purged content.

- **Never push an old branch or commit back.** Pushing one would put the purged content back into this public repository's history. The tier gate checks only the files at a commit's tip, so a branch with a clean tip but old history would pass it. Whether a history check should be added is tracked in #152.
- **Save unpublished work first.** List commits that exist only in your clone with `git log --branches --not --remotes`. Turn any you need into patches (`git format-patch`), and record uncommitted changes and stashes the same way.
- **Then replace the clone.** Make a fresh clone, and re-apply your patches onto the new branches (the commit map below shows where an old commit went). Delete the old clone, because its packs, stashes and reflogs keep the purged content. Resetting branches in place (`git fetch --prune` + `git reset --hard origin/<branch>`) is not enough: other local branches, stashes and the reflog still reference the old history.
